utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is the case number IT-08-91-T, Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. Again, we have a late start due to technical problems. Apparently, the next step is going to be for us to arrange for an exorcist. Could we have appearances for today, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic, who is at the moment missing but will be back in the courtroom, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence this morning, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So I assume the usher is going to escort the witness into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before I invite Mr. Cvijetic to begin his cross-examination, I would remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Witness. That's how I'll have to call you. My name is Slobodan Cvijetic, and I appear here as co-counsel for Mr. Stanisic. I have a few questions for you. But before I do, let me ask the usher -- let me ask the usher, please, to hand to you a file with exhibits that I intended to show to you. However, I don't know what's going on, on the Prosecution side. Lately, they are leaving us short of work and we have fewer and fewer documents and exhibits. They have already shown you most of the exhibits and asked most of the questions that I had on my list, so I believe, ultimately, we will finish this sooner than we had planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The Chamber appreciates the co-operation between the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Witness, you don't have to open documents now. We'll look at a few of them towards the end. First, I have a few general questions. In view of the fact that you are not a lawyer and you are not even a trained policeman, you have not been to the School for Internal Affairs, I will skip questions related to interpretation of legislation, although they are my favourite. Instead, I will try to elicit from you a summary of your evidence so far. To begin with, the arming of civilians in the area of Vlasenica. You said that there was an escalation of tensions, resulting in an atmosphere where you could feel already that war was in the offing and civilians of both Bosniak and Serbian ethnicity started arming themselves; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When you explained the operation of arms distribution, in answering the Prosecutor's question you distinguished between the legality and illegality of this operation, saying that this operation was geared mainly at the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think I said exactly that. This operation was geared at the entire population at first. However, later it turned out that it was mainly Muslims who handed over weapons, even those who had licenses for their weapons, and those who did not have licenses did not hand over weapons in great numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I would like to define. What does "illegal possession" mean? Serbs received weapons by responding to the mobilisation call-up and being issued with weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The Muslims obtained weapons by buying them or procuring them through other channels that had nothing to do with the mobilisation or response to the official military authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I would add that military-aged Muslims also had the possibility to obtain, legally, military equipment, including weapons, but in 1991 their own authorities forbade them to respond to mobilisation, and they abided by that decision. So they procured weapons by other means.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, concerning the legality or illegality of this arming, I believe an opinion -- a legal interpretation was even required from the Court before this operation proceeded in order to get a definitive view on what legal and illegal arming is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that happened a bit later, when, in keeping with our duties under the Law on Internal Affairs, we wanted to file criminal complaints against people for illegal possession of weapons. We consulted the president of the Court, what exactly we should do, and he gave us the explanation that we've just heard; namely, that members of the army who responded to the mobilisation call-up legally and legitimately obtained army-issue weapons, and these were mainly Serbs, whereas Muslims who did not want to respond to the mobilisation call-up but were found to own automatic weapons or other illegal equipment, were qualified as owners of illegal weapons and, thus, subject to prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation. Let me just invoke the orders that the Prosecution had exhibited. These are materials that you provided to the Prosecution upon your arrival in The Hague. This concerns the operation from the early April days, which you said was carried out without any casualties, without application of force. You said that it was done on the orders of the Territorial Defence Staff and that, basically, that, too, was a military action; am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to that order, the task was given also to the civilian police. But if I read the order well, it was within the purview of the civilian police only to make a record of illegally-owned weapons and owners, and that was your job, that was the way you proceeded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: There was a subsequent action that you discussed, the attack on Drum village on 16 June. You said it was a very different and purely military operation; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you now about the escalation of tensions in the Vlasenica municipality. Let me ask you specifically: Along the information and news you received from other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, news about attacks on military columns, the cut-off of communications with Tuzla, and with the arrival of now Serb refugees from Muslim-held territories, contributed to this escalation of tensions; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, tensions grew, and this balance of departures and arrivals soon reached 50:50. Muslims were leaving and Serbs were coming in, but as time passed ever larger numbers of Serbs arrived in Vlasenica. And the Crisis Staff thereupon formed an agency that provided accommodation for them in now vacant houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: During this escalation of tensions, you continued to work with your Muslim colleagues. Did they ask you how they should act in a situation like that? Did you discuss it with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot put a precise date on it, but the last night we had a joint patrol was around the 20th of April. I was in that patrol with two Bosniak colleagues, and we were carrying out these checks that I discussed already. And we discussed the general situation, because something was in the offing, something was in the air. Everyone could feel it. Already on the 9th of April, there was an incursion by Arkan's men not far from us, and it was logical to expect it might happen to us as well. We were still hoping that we would come out of it unscathed, but we were still thinking what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did they ask you for advise, as a friend and a colleague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my family was still there, unlike many other Serbs who had already moved their families to safety. They asked me, Are you going to move your family? I said, Well, I don't intend to so far. And, indeed, I moved my family only one month into the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, did you advise them to sort of move away, just in case, until you see what exactly is going to happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I said that's what they should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: After all these years, would you give them the same advice? Just a, Yes, or, No, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, because one needs to place one's family in a safe place before anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We'll move to the next subject. That's the take-over of power on 22 April 1992. You've already discussed it, but I have a few additional questions. Who, specifically, disarmed the police station, including you and Muslim officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That group or paramilitary group, whatever I should call them. I only later learnt that they were members of the Serbian Guard from Sekovici. Whether they were legally recruited and mobilised and attached to a proper military unit, I don't know, but it was them who carried out that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The night before that, you were on patrol with your Muslim colleague, and you had no inkling of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you were also taken by surprise when this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You should observe a pause between question and answer so the interpreters can follow. We should not overlap. It follows from your statement that you claim that up to the 15th of May, 1992, you had absolutely no control whatsoever, including physical control, over the developments in the Public Security Station in Vlasenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In mid-May, when you turned up at the station, you found two closed packages. A platoon of military police that the government had renamed from the TO Detachment into the Special Police Platoon, that's one package, and you find a mobilised unit of the police reserve; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You had no influence over either of these units; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You said that you noticed those reserve policemen were completely unusable for regular police work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I meant, rather, the special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You started coming regularly to work from mid-July 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And you got a formal decision from the minister on the 8th of August, 1992, appointing you chief of the station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a provisional decision, pending the adoption of the enactment on internal organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The person who was chief until then, Mr. Bjelanovic, on the orders of the government of the Serbian Autonomous Region Birac-Romanija, is tasked with establishing a public security station in Milici or, rather, co-ordinating this establishment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was appointed, although I didn't see the appointment, co-ordinator for the Birac region.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So, formally, the Public Security Station of Vlasenica was chief-less until the 8th of August, formally speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in July, I did some work --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the formal side of things.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally, there was no chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You also touched upon another subject; namely, the strength of the local authorities in SAO Romanija, from the point of view of a regular citizen. You will agree with me that it was a period when the central authorities of Republika Srpska, and that includes the hierarchy and the subordination within the MUP, had a hard time reaching the grass root level in all areas of Republika Srpska, due to the resistance by local authorities and their wish to hold on to positions they had acquired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's what I explained previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that quite some time was needed for the central authorities to take on and to reach every last public security station on the ground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In order to achieve that, the ministry first had to deal with the large number of problems, starting with the decision on the seat of the ministry, providing adequate equipment and staff, establishing an efficient system of communications, financing, et cetera; am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was a very tall order, but intensive work was done at that time and the results were finally achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we agree that only when the MUP seat was moved to Bijeljina, optimal prerequisites were provided for the ministry to work efficiently throughout the territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, conditions were much better once they moved to Bijeljina and the ministry was able to operate throughout the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I shall now move to another subject that you also talked a lot about yesterday, answering the Prosecutor's questions. It is about these collection centres, the holding centres. You were quite precise in that regard, but we need to clarify some things. You already said that they were not within the jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Interior, nor in your jurisdiction. There is no dispute about that; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You said that the local Secretariat of National Defence, which was later renamed the Ministry of Defence, had mobilised the reserve police force and directed it to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I noticed on the payrolls that these reserve policemen were given their salaries according to the days spent at work; that it was not a regular pay like the regular policemen received, but it depended on the number of days spent at work. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, can I just ask a clarifying question here. Your last question was that the Ministry of Defence had mobilised the reserve police force and directed the local police force to the witness, and the witness answered, Yes. Is that a correct interpretation of your question and the answer? I mean, the question that I have is: Why would the Ministry of Defence suddenly have the power to re-subordinate the reserve police force to the MUP? I thought that the reserve police force, in any case, would be under the authority of the MUP. So maybe I have missed the testimony yesterday and misunderstood, but I need a clarification of: Why would it be the Ministry of Defence who would suddenly have the authority to re-subordinate the reserve police force to the MUP? That sounds to me to be backwards somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will not testify. I shall let the witness explain. I believe that the witness did clarify this yesterday, and I shall ask him to do it once again. I understood what he said yesterday. I shall now ask him to kindly repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Perhaps there was a misinterpretation or a mistranslation, but basically in order for a reserve policeman or reserve policemen to be mobilised into the station, the Ministry of Defence, at the request of the Public Security Station, to the effect that the station needs five or ten or so policemen, the ministry -- the police sends to the ministry this number of policemen who become reserve policemen. And when they are taken over by the Ministry of the Interior, i.e., by the police, they become members of that Public Security Station. The essence is that the Ministry of Defence sends to us, at our request, as many policemen as they can, some reserve policemen that already possess certain knowledge about work in the police, because they had served time in the military -- served in the military as reserve policemen or something similar, and people who, of course, are not criminals or anything similar. So the ministry would thus respond to a request of the Public Security Station. Once they were assigned to the Public Security Station, they would become a member of that security station's reserve police force, and they would from then on be under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification, and, obviously, I have misunderstood. But let me just ask one question more. Was this related to the fact that a state of imminent threat of war had been declared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood your question correctly, this procedure of mobilising reserve policemen also existed prior to the declaration of imminent threat of war. The same procedure was applied, and we continued to apply that procedure in order to obtain a certain number of members of the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So, in essence, just to be clear now, any mobilisation of reserve police forces would, in any case, be determined by the Ministry of Defence, upon the request from an SJB or a CSB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now it is completely clear to us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So we were talking about the DSAs and the payrolls. Please assist me. It was the Secretariat of National Defence that mobilised these reserve policemen. Who actually provided the funds for them? You talked about the salaries of regular policemen yesterday, how you would send a request to the financial section of the ministry, et cetera. But for these --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was also the Ministry of the Interior that provided the wages for these policemen. Once they became members of the reserve force of the Public Security Station, their wages would be paid by the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Was there a possibility -- was there a provision made for funds to be remunerated from the Ministry of the Interior to the other ministry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In connection with the security provided for these collection centres, the need arose for guards to be provided to secure the prison, and you say that you were not -- that you were not in charge of that. And later a similar need arose in connection with the Susica camp. You never stated that you had assigned the reserve policemen to provide security at these facilities by an order, so was it the ministry, on the basis of a request of the people in charge of the camp, that assigned some guards to provide security there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the security for Susica, the police never provided security, nor assigned any members to guard -- any of its members to guard this facility. The Susica camp was set up by the municipal organs initially, and later it was taken over by the army, meaning that the Territorial Defence Staff assigned the people to provide security for that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. You also referred to the fact that patrols of the police station escorted the buses with the people who expressed a wish to leave the territory. Namely, up to Kladanj there existed groups which recognised no authorities, including the military authorities, and the danger was that they could attack the convoys?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but let me just explain. The police escorted the buses not up to Kladanj, but up to a point where there was a tunnel leading to Kladanj, because on the other end of the tunnel the territory was already under the control of B and H forces, whether it was BH Police, or the Green Berets, or somebody else. So the buses would come to the tunnel. The people would disembark and pass on foot through the tunnel and be received on the other end. This happened every day until the 15th of May until the day when the Tuzla column incident happened. After that, the tunnel was mined, it was blown up on the Kladanj side, so that people could no longer pass in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I will now show you a document. It is already a court exhibit. It's number is P160, and I believe that it is on page 26 in both the English and Serbo-Croat-Bosnian versions. Until we have what we need on the screen: You often refer to the Tuzla column. What are you referring to? You're referring to the attack on the military convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I'm referring to, because that is when the character of the war in B and H changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Who attacked whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the then TO Tuzla attacked a JNA military column.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So the Muslim forces attacked them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbian version, we have to turn to the next page. And in the English, we are on the right page. The next page. We need the conclusion under number 13 to mirror the English page. So it is the next page in the Serbian. That is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, please have a look at this section. I will tell you what document is in question. You were not present at the first collegium meeting of MUP officers held in Belgrade, where far-reaching and diverse tasks were actually drawn -- made conclusions about. Inter alia, you see, in item 13, the first bullet, they had noted the problem of the actions of paramilitary formations, and the centres were assigned the task to follow that phenomenon, to submit reports and information to the MUP on it. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of a meeting of this kind having been held on the 11th of July, 1992, in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that it was held. I was not present, and I did not have occasion to study this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Please tell me now, in that period did you, either through orders, or the ministry's documents, or through your chief, or the chief of the Centre of Security Services, were you informed about the need to combat paramilitary units and that work had to be done along those lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because there was intensive work going on against such paramilitary units and against all negative phenomena of this kind. It was us from the field, actually, that exerted pressure on the chief of the centre in order for them to find a way for these paramilitary units to be disbanded and sent away, removed, in a legitimate and legal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If we -- even if we took this date as the beginning of this activity, although we do have evidence that it had started earlier, you will agree that this activity started in the beginning of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the beginning of July. As I mentioned yesterday, even before this we had occasion to clash with paramilitary units, to disarm them, and similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now I will show you another document. It is also a court document. It is Exhibit P591. It is page 3 in the Serbian version. In the meantime, we shall also see what page in the English version it is. We are unable to find the proper English page, but it is page 3, paragraph 2, in the Serbian version, which says: "Currently in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are about 50 paramilitary formations." It is also on page 3 of the English, paragraph 1. So: "60 paramilitary units of a total strength of about 4.000 to 5.000 men, of which we shall list but the most important." So -- and then it goes on to enumerate them. Among the strongest, in the very next paragraph, they refer to the Yellow Wasps, with 170 people, et cetera. Can you read that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is the Intelligence Administration of the Main Staff of the Army of the SR of B and H, and this is their report dated the 28th of July, 1992. Mr. Witness, I showed you this for the sole purpose that we agree that the problem of paramilitary units was not a minor problem and that these were, indeed, well-organised and numerous units. Do you agree with my position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will also agree with me when I say that in order to deal with such a problem, the ministry had to organise its own ranks well and to undertake thorough preparations, to actually train a special unit for that particular purpose, as well as to co-ordinate this action and link up its efforts with the military police as well as with you in the field. I believe that you told us that you, yourself, gave 30 of your men to participate in one of these actions. Do you agree with me that comprehensive, extensive preparations had to be undertaken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This operation, in its preparation, implied a degree of secrecy; it was not to be known that it was being prepared?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can we now have 1D176. In your file, tab 13. Let's just see the English. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is an order from the minister of the interior, dated 27 July 1992. Please pay attention to page 1. Mr. Stanisic is now carrying out in practice all the conclusions of the meeting in Belgrade. Among other things, in item 2, he recalls his order to remove all those who were responsible for crimes before taking up duty and in the course of their duty. Do you see that in item 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In item 3, he says that any surplus of such individuals should be referred to the army, and you said surpluses were turned over to the army, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Read also item 4. All the units set up during the war -- all special units formed during the war should be immediately disbanded and placed under the command of the army. You said that was the case with that special unit, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then the same item further below, as well as item 5, speaks of the replenishment of the Special Detachment of the Police and the way it will be manned. Now we need item 7 on the next page. In English, too, we need the next page. We still don't see the English. Please read item 7, sir. You will agree with me that within the framework of activities from the beginning of July until 27 July, the action to disband and eliminate paramilitary units continues, and a direct order is now issued that they be removed from the territory of Republika Srpska; am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I was directly involved in this work.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need the document anymore. Now, tell me, even before the action in Zvornik, you personally disarmed a paramilitary unit called Charlie's Men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You did that before the action in Zvornik; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The action in Zvornik followed after this order; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That is to say, after the 27th of July, the action in Zvornik occurred; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that after the action in Zvornik, that special unit went to Bratunac and then to Foca with the same assignment -- on the same assignment; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that before the action in Zvornik, this unit had been in Brcko and Bijeljina on the same assignment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware, but I didn't have particular information. I know that it worked in other areas as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will now agree with me that this was, in fact, a systematic, comprehensive operation to eliminate a negative phenomenon, namely, the paramilitary units, and it cannot be associated with individual incidents; it is, on the contrary, a result of a general intention to remove this negative phenomenon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I hope the witness can answer that question, Mr. Cvijetic, because that was a combination of a question and submissions and a number of things. But I suppose he'd have a go at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can divide the question into a number of questions. I'm sorry, but the witness answered already.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'll have to rephrase. You will agree with me that this action in Zvornik was just one in a series of planned actions aimed at eliminating paramilitary formations in a broader area; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now part 2. You will agree with me that we cannot associate it with any individual incident caused by a paramilitary unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the incidents that occurred can just be cited as an example of their negative impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But the point is, it was the general position of the ministry that they should be eliminated and removed from Republika Srpska, either by placing them under the command of military authorities or by expelling them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, because without a definitive decision and position of the ministry, the ultimate goal, to expel them, would not have been possible to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that the ministry displayed persistence, courage, and consistency, and the action continued throughout 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I believe I will be able to finish before the break. Let me just try to clarify something that left me in confusion yesterday. Could you just confirm that there was never any incident between Mr. Stanisic, personally, and any paramilitary units, specifically the Yellow Wasps? And the incident you described yesterday is known to us as an incident involving the minister of information, Velibor Ostojic. I would therefore ask you: Do you allow the possibility that you were slightly confused about this? The young man who came to you and said that the minister was experiencing problems, did he perhaps mean his minister, whereas you understood it as meaning your minister?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now I'm confused too. I know that I had reports. There was a series of incidents, beginning with citizens who were intercepted, beaten up, their cars and their money were robbed, up to members of the leadership who were the victims of such incidents. I remember something like that with Velibor Ostojic. This was at a stage of preparation of these activities. That young man who came by told this story, that this intensive activity will follow, and he said even the minister had problems of the kind. And that's how I understood it -- or misunderstood it. If Mr. Stanisic had been mistreated, himself, then that would have been the straw that broke the camel's back, but I wasn't necessarily right in that understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So I understand that you allow the possibility the young man meant another minister, and you understood him as referring to Minister Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And just for your information, I will tell you that the young men who were Mr. Stanisic's bodyguards in 1992 - he had one driver and one security man - were called Zoran Jasarevic and Goran Abazovic. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Goran -- I knew that he had a security detail at the time, but I didn't know these young men personally, although, of course, I appreciated them and they appreciated me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: For procedural reasons, I have to put to you another fact before I conclude. It was only in 1994 that a young man by the name of Dusko Malovic was employed in Mr. Stanisic's security detail; do you allow for that possibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allow for that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I have to mention this because you were there when the minister came back in 1994, and you were able to see that young man by his side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before the break, I have concluded. Thank you, Witness. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvijetic. Mr. Pantelic, do you have any questions of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we don't have a question for this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What we'll do is take the break now and then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We will take the break now, and, Mr. Olmsted, you would begin your re-examination when we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We apologise for any inconvenience to counsel caused by our delay in resuming the Bench, but it was occasioned by one of those ancillary matters that invariably engage Judges. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Shall we wait for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, I believe it was the day before yesterday you testified that the SDS was arming the Serb population back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us, is it legal for a political party to be arming the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify your position, is it your position that after the take-over in April 1992, that every Serb who possessed a weapon possessed it legally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not all of them possessed weapons legally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to further clarify your position, is it your position that only persons mobilised into the Serb military were committing crimes against the Muslim population in Vlasenica after the take-over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood your question correctly, the persons who were mobilised into the RS Army included the smallest group responsible for such crimes. It is other groups that were mainly responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So only military soldiers were responsible for committing crimes against the Muslims; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I can be of assistance. I wasn't listening to the translation, but apparently the transcript doesn't show what the witness has answered. Maybe you can clarify, because I believe there is a misunderstanding between -- between what the witness said and what is entered into the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Put your question to the witness again, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me ask you the question again, just to make sure we got the record correct. I want to clarify your position on the issue of crimes against the Muslim population after the take-over. Is it your position that only persons in the military -- persons who were mobilised into the military were committing crimes against the Muslim population in Vlasenica after the take-over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, my position is that most crimes were committed by paramilitaries and informal groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the special police unit at SJB Vlasenica, were members of this special police unit mobilised through the Secretariat of National Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mobilised through the Secretariat for National Defence into Territorial Defence. After that, the Crisis Staff made a decision that this unit should be seconded to the Public Security Station after the VRS was established. Why? Because they did not want to join the VRS as an organised unit, and they could not exist as a separate unit outside the army or the police, so they got the Crisis Staff to decide that this unit be seconded to the Public Security Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: After this special police unit was seconded to the SJB Vlasenica, any additional members to join that unit would have been mobilised from the -- by the Secretariat of National Defence into the police, itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, today the question was asked whether you had no influence over the special unit, and that's at page 8, lines 3 through 4. By this, did you mean that the Crisis Staff imposed upon you the special unit; is that what you meant by "no influence"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of mobilisation, and when the decision was made to second this unit to the Public Security Station, I was unable to have a say or influence that decision. It was adopted anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify, that decision was made by the Crisis Staff in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And once they were within the SJB Vlasenica, you had the power to discipline them; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but at that time the only measure that could be taken against them was to remove them and send them to VRS units. However, it would often happen that those men whom we wanted to remove and send to the army left Republika Srpska because they didn't want to join either the army or the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, certainly, you could have filed a criminal report against them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, we've been discussing this for three days. We were working within the Criminal Code, and we did all we could to prosecute such cases. We documented and filed reports in every case where we were able to. We forwarded a number of such cases to the Prosecutor's Office, and the Prosecutor's Office did not exist until July or August. And it is common practice that the prosecutor could ask a criminal report to be supplemented or rejected, but they had no obligation to inform us of what they decided. We had no feedback from the Prosecutor's Office. We didn't know what happened with our criminal report, whether it was rejected or not. From our viewpoint, from our position in the police, we did all we could to document these cases and file them to the prosecutor. Another line of work -- another aspect of documenting such cases is sending reports. When the Military Prosecutor's Office and the Military Court were established, we did that, too. Anything that could be found in official notes and reports that went to the ministry, these criminal complaints were either sent to the civilian prosecutor or the military prosecutor. If you wanted to see where the thing hit a snag or what failed to work, you should look in the records of these institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That was a very long answer to a pretty straightforward question. But am I correct that, yes, in fact, you could file criminal reports against members of the special unit if you had information they committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we would file such reports, and we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I need to show you a document. It's 65 ter 1552. And I ask that this not be broadcast, the reason being it's a log-book from the Prosecution's Office in Vlasenica and it contains names of victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: This arises out of cross-examination how?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The witness just said that the Prosecutor's Office was not functioning until July or August, and I just want him to take a look at the prosecutor's log-book and see if that's the case. So it arises out of his last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But it's the prosecutor's log-book, not his?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, but if he can identify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you have anticipated my objections. I never dealt with this question at all, and it does not arise from the examination of this witness. The Prosecutor is broaching a new subject which, in fact, was already clarified yesterday, and your intervention is quite appropriate and I subscribe to it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, in his last response, when we were talking about his authority over the special unit, which was raised during cross-examination, he says that he wasn't filing criminal reports because -- against the special police because the Prosecutor's Office wasn't functioning. And I need to show him a document to show that it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, but the difficulty I see, Mr. Olmsted, is that you are seeking to contradict this witness on a document that he has nothing to do with. It may very -- that document, standing on its own, may very well, when put alongside the witness's testimony, indicate that the witness's testimony in this regard is inaccurate, but I don't know that it is -- that you can lay that plank down in the manner that you propose now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So if I understand Your Honour correctly, the issue is whether he can -- he has the necessary foundation to talk about this particular log-book?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No. What you were seeking to do, as I understand it, is to challenge or confront the witness as to the accuracy of his last answer to you. When I say "last answer," before this issue has arisen. But you are seeking to do that not on the basis of work product of the witness, but of somebody else. So apart from the fact that you're entering into new territory which wasn't raised in cross-examination, at the end of this exercise all you would have achieved is getting the witness's comment on something that somebody else did. So it isn't going to be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, respectfully, the reason I'm showing him this document is to see whether he would revise his answer, based upon what he sees in front of the computer screen. If he wants to stick to his position, then that's fine. And, I think, well, at least in the judicial system I come from, that is an appropriate way to approach a topic such as this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, I thought the witness had answered to your question, about whether or not they did file complaints, in the positive. He said, Yes, we did, in fact, file complaints. So that would seem to exhaust the purpose of this extra exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, then I'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, if you did file criminal reports against members of the special police, those would be in your Vlasenica crime register; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When you reviewed your crime register the other day, did you see any of those criminal reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we focused solely on the segment under Article 213, I did not pay attention. But the crime register shows that it was not only illegal possession of weapons that were the crimes, but there were also different offences by members of all ethnicities. As far as I remember now -- in fact, I cannot remember now, of the 182 offences in the crime register, which one was under what article and by whom. It is a fact, however, that in those impossible conditions, the wartime conditions, we did everything in our power to make the institution function properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, we see, from the payroll records for May 1992 that we showed you the other day, that you signed them as chief of the station, and you also paid yourself a higher salary than the other police officers. And you also testified yesterday that these payroll went from you to the CSB and then on to the Ministry of the Interior. Were you misrepresenting your position as chief on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have clarified over the past two days in what position I had been and at what time, when it was that I was formally appointed chief and from which time I could consider myself a co-ordinator. That was sometime in mid-July, after serious talks and consultations with Mr. Cvijetic. Until that time, I had been seconded by the former Ministry of the Interior and worked there as such. The previous chief, my colleague Bjelanovic, would delegate to me certain powers to enable me to carry out certain tasks which were of no bearing on the strategy, so to speak, of the ministry, i.e., of the police station that he had been in charge of. Why did he do this? Why did he delegate such powers to me? At that time, I was the only worker -- worker taking over from the former Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with work experience in the Ministry of the Interior, with a proper professional exam, and the only worker with -- with adequate university qualifications. It was in order for me to contribute as much as possible to the establishment of the structure of the police station in order for the police station to start functioning in keeping with the Law on Internal Affairs and in keeping with the rules emanating from that particular law, which I later did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's move on. You stated today that there were no police guards at Susica camp. What about Dragan Nikolic? He was a member of the special police unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic left when the collection centre started functioning. The TO took him over, as part of their organisation, to provide security for the collection centre. I cannot recall at this point on what grounds he featured on that list, was he retained on it in order for him to be able to receive his salary at that time or was it for another reason, but I claim with full responsibility from the month of May he was not a member of either the reserve force, or of the special unit, or of anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. I think your position on that issue is quite clear now. Would -- while the Susica camp was open, would the police still patrol the Susica area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That stems from the organisation and the Rules of Service of the police. Namely, the police worked upon the principle of sector patrols. Every chief of a patrol sector had the task to follow the security situation in his respective sector, meaning that the chief of the patrol sector and the policeman in the patrol in charge of that particular area would occasionally drop in on the guards and inquire about the matters which are within police competence; namely, whether there were any problems, whether they had any information that some attacks had happened, that people were not assembling around the camp, or information to that effect. That was all -- that was in the remit of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if there was a person held at Susica camp that the police needed to interview, they're able to bring those persons to the police station to interview them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only according to a request and a permit issued by the competent authority in charge of the collection centre which later was a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yesterday, you testified that Bosniaks left the municipality in large numbers after the take-over of the municipality. By August, let's say, how many Muslims remained in Vlasenica? This will lead to a question that will directly relate to cross-examination, if I may ask this foundational question. By August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: By August, I cannot tell you the exact number, but let's say about 30 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just to clarify, 30 per cent of the Muslim population remained or had left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Remained. It is a relevant figure, but approximately so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is the question that comes out of cross-examination: There was a lot of talk about the paramilitaries and all these operations to contain them, to expel them from the municipality, or incorporate them into the VRS. Can you tell us, were the paramilitaries -- what were they doing to the Serbian population that was in Vlasenica? Were they causing any problems with the Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. It would happen, for example, that they would disturb the public law and order by shooting, by throwing grenades, by barging into people's flats. When they were no longer interested in Bosniak flats and houses, they would break into Serb houses and flats, and different forms of looting is also what they did, plunder. They created problems of all sorts. Namely, they created problems for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Final topic with regard to the Yellow Wasps. During your interview last year, would you agree that without the Prosecution Office asking you a particular question regarding this event, that you told us about Minister Stanisic coming through Vlasenica and you speaking to his driver about what happened to Minister Stanisic at the hands of the Yellow Wasps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but now, in hindsight, taking into account the time distance of some 18 years, and taking into account that I already said yesterday that we did not have -- that we had less communication with Sarajevo than in peacetime, I did not know those guys. It is true that this lad came, and you saw that I actually had mistaken their identity -- I mean, their names, but, anyway, this lad came and he said that an action was in the offing, that was under preparation, and that they had problems in Zvornik with the Yellow Wasps. Within that framework and a series of incidents that I already was aware of, and I have already said that anyone had to pass through Vlasenica, anyone going from Pale to Sarajevo, and people had already complained that they had been looted, their cars and valuables seized and robs, and other problems as well. I knew that a few days particular that, Minister Ostojic had also had a problem. So this man, when he came, he said -- this lad, Even Minister Stanisic has had a problem. An action is being prepared to break up these groups. I didn't want to tell him that I was already aware, that already "au courant" with all these activities, but I told him that I would be only too happy to help disband -- these paramilitary units and for somebody to put an end to their activities, and for them to see that they cannot go on doing what they were doing, and that they would have to either join the army or disband. That is the gist of that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And with regard to your interview last year, do you agree that you told us, again without being prompted, that the person -- the driver that you spoke to was by the name of Malovic, and this young man got killed later on in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-179 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They actually mixed up the names of these lads. But as Minister Stanisic had also his second term, this other lad was part of his security guard during his second term in 1993 or 1994. That's why I mixed them up. In 1992, a certain Goran Abazovic, whom I personally know, was part of his security detail, and this other guy whom I don't personally know, and that's how I got things mixed up. So Malovic was part of Minister Stanisic's bodyguards in 1993 or 1994, and later, as far as I know, he got killed somewhere in Belgrade or in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we thank you for your assistance to the Tribunal. You are now released, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And with that, we take the adjournment. We resume in this courtroom at 2.15 on Monday afternoon. I wish everyone a safe weekend. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 15th day of March, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.41 a.m.,
